title: The Nuniya of Urwa ibn Hizam
intro: Urwa calls to two companions at Sana'a to take him towards the homes of Afra, the cousin he grew up with and hoped to marry. Al-Qali quotes Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari explaining that transmitters agreed on some verses of the Nuniya and that he combined their wording. An ailing body, a homesick camel and two baffled healers all find their way into Urwa’s account of the separation. One verse also travels, with a different rhyme, in Majnun Layla’s Mu'nisa.

translation: My two friends of the noblest of Hilal ibn Amir,
turn aside today at Sana'a and wait for me.
1.sharh: He addresses two men of high standing by their tribal descent. Before he can ask for the journey he really wants, he must persuade them to slow down.

translation: Do not begrudge the reward you may earn through me. Be kind.
It is with me that you are tested today.
2.sharh: Looking after him offers the travellers a reward. The sufferer is the occasion of the trial, but the choice being tested is theirs.

translation: You both know that in all al-Markh there is
no brother or faithful friend. Then leave me be.
3.sharh: He searches a whole district for someone who would act as a brother. His abrupt dismissal already shows how quickly his need for company can turn into hurt.

translation: Must you aim at her country every day
with two eyes whose very pupils are drowning?
4.sharh: He takes aim at her country with his eyes. The tiny dark figure called the ‘person of the eye’ in Arabic is drowning in each pupil just as he tries to see.

translation: Then carry me, God bless you both,
to the encampment at al-Rawha, and leave me there.
5.sharh: The blessing softens his earlier dismissal. They need not look after him for ever if they will only deliver him to the people camped at al-Rawha.

translation: On a tall, strong-backed camel that speeds through the night,
crossing the broad waste at a long, quick stride.
6.sharh: The request for a lift now becomes precise about the animal. A camel built for a long night march can cross the wide ground her rider cannot manage alone.

translation: Call briefly on Afra. Tomorrow you both
will own how far the road and separation reach.
7.sharh: He asks only for a passing visit. Tomorrow the two men who could make it possible will have to admit the full distance that parting opens up.

translation: You two who carry tales of Afra, leave me one look
to gladden my eyes, then leave me to myself.
8.sharh: Even the men who report on the lovers are asked for a small mercy. A single look would settle the eyes that a moment ago could see nothing through tears.

translation: Have you been taken in by this shirt I wear,
new, and these two fine Yemeni mantles?
9.sharh: Fine clothes can make a sick traveller look prosperous and well. He names the new shirt and the two bright mantles as the misleading evidence his friends have seen.

translation: Lift the shirt from me and you will see plainly
what Afra has made me suffer, young men.
10.sharh: He asks the young men to verify his account for themselves. The shirt separates a public appearance of health from proof that can be seen immediately underneath.

translation: You will recognise a little flesh, thin bones,
and a heart that never stops beating wildly.
11.sharh: Two things in his body have dwindled and one has grown more insistent. The last verse will return to the beating first registered here under the shirt.

translation: Love of Afra has left a sore on my liver.
Both my eyes drip for longing for her.
12.sharh: Grief has an inward lesion and an outward sign. The liver is a seat of intense feeling in this poetry, and the eyes give away what the body keeps hidden.

translation: Of all people Afra is the one whose love I most hope for.
Afra is the one who turns away and takes her time.
13.sharh: Her name opens both halves, holding his best hope and his disappointment together. The masculine description in the second can mean ‘the person who turns away’, as an early commentator explains.

translation: If only every two who love each other,
of humankind or herd, could meet,
14.sharh: His private wish extends to any two attached creatures, even the beasts of the herd. Shortly the camel beneath him will have a longing quite as real as his own.

translation: so one beloved might have what they need from the other,
and my Lord watch over them unseen.
15.sharh: He imagines divinely protected privacy for the pair. Seeing one another and being seen by outsiders have opposite values in a world of informers.

translation: My camel’s longing lies behind me, mine ahead.
She and I pull different ways.
16.sharh: Rider and mount share a word for desire and disagree about the road. Every step towards his destination carries her further from her own.

translation: My love is ahead. I have no turning place behind.
My young camel longs south for Yemen in the morning.
17.sharh: ‘Ahead’ belongs to the rider’s purpose. His young mount starts each morning of the same journey with her affections fixed on Yemen behind them.

translation: My love is Iraqi. She bends her rein
towards a Yemeni flash when the stars appear.
18.sharh: His own compass points to Iraq. A flash on the Yemeni horizon turns the animal’s head towards the rain and pasture it may promise at home.

translation: Take on my longing as well as your own and you will limp.
You have no hands for such a heavy load.
19.sharh: He tries his grief out as an extra pack on her back. ‘No two hands for it’ is an idiom for being unequal to a task, with an added oddity when addressed to a camel.

translation: Ah, our two livers, how they tremble in fear of separation’s
burn, and of the turns that distance takes.
20.sharh: The rider and the camel now possess one aching organ apiece. Their destinations differ, but the verse gives their fear a single bodily rhythm.

translation: We were both afraid the dwellings might grow far apart,
afraid the staff would split and parting come.
21.sharh: He remembers an earlier apprehension shared by two. A single staff splitting supplied Arabic with an image for an alliance or a life together breaking apart.

translation: My companions say when they take me to task,
“An Iraqi longing, and you a man of Yemen?”
22.sharh: The friends turn two directions on a compass into a reproach. They treat the mismatch between his address and his desire as something he ought to correct.

translation: A Yemeni is no companion for Iraq,
yet a turn of time may bring the two together.
23.sharh: He grants the geography and holds out for time. The same changes of fortune that separated two people might one day bring them together.

translation: I have borne from Afra what neither I
nor the mountains rooted in the earth have strength for.
24.sharh: He has already borne a weight he declares beyond him. Even mountains fixed fast in the earth are drawn into that contradiction between endurance and capacity.

translation: It is as though a sandgrouse hung by its wing
from my liver, so fiercely does it beat.
25.sharh: A bird suspended by one wing must beat hard with the other. That desperate movement gives the reader something more exact than a general description of pain.

translation: I offered the healer of al-Yamama his own price,
and the healer of Najd, if they cured me.
26.sharh: The two healers may name their fee. The only term Urwa sets is recovery, and that will prove to be the term neither expert can meet.

translation: They said, “Yes, we cure every sickness,”
and rose eagerly with the people visiting me.
27.sharh: Their first diagnosis admits no exceptions. The visitors at the sickbed form an audience for a confident promise the two will later have to withdraw.

translation: They left no charm they knew untried,
no potion for forgetting they did not give me.
28.sharh: They try spoken remedies as well as something he can drink to forget. The exhaustive list makes their eventual failure a limit of their art.

translation: Yet they did not cure the sickness in me entirely.
They held nothing back, nor spared themselves for me.
29.sharh: A failed cure gives him no grounds to accuse the healers. He is as precise about their effort as he is about the persistence of his pain.

translation: They said, “May God heal you. By God, we have
no strength for what your ribs enclose.”
30.sharh: The healers’ claim gives way to a prayer. They borrow the ‘two hands’ formula already used of the camel, the lover and the mountains.

translation: I left the healer with my turban slipping
off my head, my fingers unable to wind it back.
31.sharh: The long medical episode ends in a small failure of movement. He cannot do the ordinary work of his fingers and wind his slipping turban.

translation: Beside me are two true friends when I lean over,
two balancing loads at the flanks of my worn mount.
32.sharh: The companions steady him like balanced packs on either side of a worn camel. Friendship becomes something that can literally keep a sick man in the saddle.

translation: Uncle, you breaker of faith, may you always be tried,
bound fast to trouble and humiliation.
33.sharh: The true companions give way to the uncle who broke faith. Urwa assigns his kinsman a companion of his own, enduring trouble.

translation: You betrayed me. Treachery was in your nature.
You fastened this ceaseless beating to my heart.
34.sharh: A broken undertaking has acquired a pulse. Urwa moves from the uncle’s act to his character and then to the beat that must be endured in someone else’s body.

translation: You bequeathed me distress, anguish and regret.
You bequeathed my eye tears that never cease.
35.sharh: An uncle might leave his kinsman something of value. This legacy has two parts, inward grief for the man and an inexhaustible flow for his eye.

translation: May you always long for the one you love,
your heart divided among places everywhere.
36.sharh: He wants the uncle to know the divided attention of a lover living far away. A heart distributed among places can be entirely at home in none.

translation: I long for the Gathering, since I have been told
that Afra and I will meet on the Day of Gathering.
37.sharh: The Day of Gathering holds an unexpectedly personal promise. He fastens on the literal sense of a gathering, the chance of occupying the same place again.

translation: You two crows of the abandoned camp, tell me plainly,
is it for a break with Afra that you mourn?
38.sharh: Crows at a deserted camp were heard as birds of parting. He asks their call for a precise answer about Afra and lends them the human sound of sobbing.

translation: If what you say is true, then go
with my flesh to your two nests and eat me.
39.sharh: If their omen is true, his life has already lost its use to him. The two birds he has treated as messengers suddenly have a very real appetite and two nests to feed.

translation: Eat me as no one has ever seen anything eaten.
Do not gnaw my sides. Swallow me whole.
40.sharh: He orders a meal without precedent. The exact distinction between nibbling away and gulping down matters because he wants no recognisable remains left behind.

translation: Let no one know what my story was.
Let no other bird taste what you leave.
41.sharh: He would deny his story to people and his remains to other birds. The crows have become his last confidants in a world where confidences travel.

translation: Can Afra forget all memory of me
when I have left a memory of her everywhere?
42.sharh: His fear of being forgotten comes up against the traces of her he has spread by speaking. This very verse adds another to the record.

translation: God curse the talebearers and their saying,
“So-and-so is now so-and-so’s sweetheart.”
43.sharh: He curses the sentence along with those who pass it on. Its two empty names let anyone in a gathering supply a fresh pair of victims.

translation: Whenever we sat somewhere we enjoyed being together,
they spread tales of us until I tired of the place.
44.sharh: Tale-bearers spoil the very place the lovers once enjoyed. Majnun’s Mu'nisa gives its last word a longer ending. Al-Zamakhshari credits this verse and the next to Ibn al-Tathriyya, reversing their order.

translation: Talebearers close in on me from every side,
when one alone would have been enough.
45.sharh: One informer could destroy his peace unaided. Making them surround him gives their numbers the physical pressure of a siege.

translation: Even if a talebearer lived away in al-Yamama,
and I guarded against his evil luck, he would find me.
46.sharh: Distance keeps Urwa from Afra yet never seems to hinder an informer. In another version the lover lives in Hadramawt, so that the spy must cross the country to find him.

translation: My uncle demands eighty young she-camels of me.
Afra, I own only eight.
47.sharh: His uncle asks for ten times the number of animals he owns. Eight and eighty are almost the same sound in Arabic, and Afra’s name falls between them.

translation: If only we could live our lives together, and when
we die, two shrouds could enfold us.
48.sharh: He imagines sharing both a life and its ending. The Arabic insists on two shrouds, one for each body, even at the closest point of his wish.

translation: If only, free of all suspicion, we were always
two untroubled creatures grazing the wild together.
49.sharh: The wish for privacy carries them beyond human society altogether. Grazing together would release them from bridewealth and scrutiny, the burdens their people impose.

translation: When we came to a watering place, its folk would shout,
“Two mangy camels, covered with scab!”
50.sharh: He would accept even the skin disease that makes herders drive strange camels from their water. The insult is in the dual: the two would still be together.

translation: By God, I never told your secret to a companion,
even a brother to me. My lips never uttered it.
51.sharh: He narrows the circle from a trusted companion to his very lips. The extravagant oath makes the tiny exception that follows all the more telling.

translation: Except that one day I did speak to my friend
in the forenoon, our two young camels striding along,
52.sharh: His exception takes several lines to tell. Before letting us hear the words, he puts the listener beside him among the moving camels.

translation: late in the morning, as a faint south wind touched us,
a breath whose fragrance set us trembling.
53.sharh: He refines the time of day and recalls the lightest touch of air. A wind all but too weak to feel has a scent powerful enough to start his pulse racing.

translation: I bore the sighs of morning. I could bear them.
For the sighs of evening I have no strength.
54.sharh: At last comes what he let slip. He gave his friend the daily rhythm of his suffering without ever pronouncing Afra’s name.

translation: Uncle, may no kinsman give you so much as a sip.
Both your feet have slipped.
55.sharh: A drink is the smallest kindness a relative can offer in travelling country. He would withhold even that from the man who lost his footing as a kinsman.

translation: You held out Afra to me till I hoped for her.
What you promised was known everywhere.
56.sharh: The promise made him hopeful well before it made him happy. Once it became public, his disappointment belonged to everyone’s conversation.

translation: My own little cousin. They came between us,
and two shrikes cried that parting was near.
57.sharh: An affectionate diminutive draws the cousin close in the act of naming her. Two shrikes then call out the separation that people have imposed.

translation: How dear the one for whose sake they blame me,
the delight of my eye and of my tongue.
58.sharh: Seeing her delights the eye and speaking of her delights the tongue. The second pleasure is one the people who keep them apart have been unable to take away.

translation: If I saw her among enemies, I would go to her.
If she saw me among enemies, she would come to me.
59.sharh: He reverses the direction of the journey in the second half. For one verse, at least, he can give Afra an answering movement as bold as his own.

translation: One who stood in awe of me, as I did of her, in everything,
though I was keener than my own spearpoint.
60.sharh: The matched verbs express reciprocal awe, a delicate balance after the crossing of enemy lines. He can be formidable elsewhere and still approach her with deference.

translation: By God, but for love of Afra those two worn
curtains of your tent would never have closed about me.
61.sharh: Love alone could induce him to live inside those two shabby tent hangings. The uncle’s household, once the setting of their childhood, closes in around him.

translation: Two threadbare scraps, loosely woven, good for nothing,
ugly, with grubs crawling through them.
62.sharh: He makes us look close enough at both hangings to see the grubs. Contempt for the uncle has found a material object it can minutely describe.

translation: Two flimsy curtains good for nothing,
clapping together whenever the winds rise.
63.sharh: The repeated judgement on the curtains now acquires a sound. Wind makes them flap against each other, exposing how little shelter the tent provides.

translation: Nor would I have followed the women’s litters in bright morning,
my saddle on a camel rising to a swift trot,
64.sharh: The oath about the uncle’s tent still governs the sentence. It took love to put him on a fast camel in pursuit of the departing litters.

translation: for Afra, when time and people gave us an unguarded hour
and our two natures yielded easily to youth.
65.sharh: He remembers catching the world off guard, when their dispositions both inclined easily to young love. A version in Ibn Muqbil’s poetry gives the young woman the name Dahma.

translation: I would draw close to a fair, slender-waisted woman,
the little daughter of a man bristling with hostility.
66.sharh: The waist is slight enough for her ornaments to shift against it. The affectionate diminutive for the girl is set beside the forbidding character of her father.

translation: When she puts on her two beaded sashes and stands,
they look like the two supple reins of a filly.
67.sharh: The sashes fall in two long lines as she stands. The filly’s pair of soft reins gives their movement a shape a traveller on horseback would recognise at once.

translation: Their meeting point bites into the garments on her body.
Their two folds hang loose and sway.
68.sharh: Where the ornaments meet they catch tightly against her clothing. Their loops are free to swing, so the eye follows the same pair from tension to slack.

translation: Below them lie two curved dunes, beaten firm together
by showers from the stars of al-Jawza.
69.sharh: Below the narrow waist he pictures the curves of two sandhills. Rain has packed their surfaces firm, setting them against the ornaments swinging freely above.

translation: Afra, how many sighs you have made me taste,
how much grief that sets the eye streaming on and on.
70.sharh: His body replaces hers in the picture. A sigh can apparently be tasted, and grief has acquired enough will of its own to keep his eye running.

translation: Whenever I climb a rise and my eyes look out
from their inner corners, both of them drip.
71.sharh: A rise in the ground should give him a better view. Instead he knows precisely where the tears will well up each time he gets there.

translation: If any lover’s two eyes ever overflowed with blood,
mine would pour it out, each racing the other.
72.sharh: Blood replaces tears in a deliberately conditional claim. Giving the two eyes a race of their own carries the poem’s fondness for pairs right into his body.

translation: Will Afra’s two camel-drivers, if I fear to lose her,
heed me and draw up when I call?
73.sharh: Hope now hangs on two working men in the caravan. If they ease their pace at his call, the distance to Afra might still be closed.

translation: They strike the slow beast at the rear when it flags,
pressing on, wary in their dislike of us.
74.sharh: The straggler would have given him a chance to catch up. Their work is to beat it forward, and in his distress he reads their vigilance as hostility.

translation: What is it with you drivers? May fever and plague
strike you both. Will you not stop?
75.sharh: The curse interrupts a plea that began politely enough. Even in wishing disease on both men, he comes back to the simple request to stop.

translation: What is it with you drivers? May you both be clothed
in tunics of pitch brought to the boil.
76.sharh: Being handed a garment sounds benign until its material is named. Shirts of pitch also recall the Qur’anic description of punishment, here turned into a traveller’s angry curse.

translation: My grief for Afra is a grief like
the edge of a spearhead against liver and entrails.
77.sharh: The spearpoint that once measured his own keenness turns inward. It gives the place and the sharpness of a pain the drivers have failed to relieve.

translation: For love of Afra, how dear to me the meeting place
of Na'am and Birk, there where they join.
78.sharh: This reading locates affection at the meeting of two places. Al-Qali also gives a version about where ‘yes’ and ‘no’ meet: in that reading the meeting place is her lips.

translation: If the most lovesick of men and his equal
among the jinn were to meet,
79.sharh: He looks for the most afflicted lover in each of two worlds. The imagined meeting prepares a comparison that even ordinary human experience cannot supply.

translation: and each told his grief, and then I told mine,
my longing would outmeasure theirs many times over.
80.sharh: He lets the human lover and the jinn speak first. Their two accounts together supply a measure that his own longing would exceed many times over.

translation: She has left me unable to take in anyone’s words,
even when I confide in him and he in me.
81.sharh: The scale abruptly contracts from humans and jinn to two people talking. Even private speech, close enough to be exchanged in confidence, cannot hold his attention.

translation: Afra has left my heart like
a crow’s wing, beating without rest.
82.sharh: The exposed heartbeat of the opening and the crows of the abandoned camp meet in this last wing. Its movement continues in the imagination after the voice comes to rest.

1.1.1.head: خَليل
1.1.1.meaning: An intimate friend. The dual addresses two fellow travellers.

1.1.3-6.head: عُليا هِلال بن عامِر
1.1.3-6.meaning: “The highest of Hilal ibn Amir”, the nobles of that tribal line.

1.2.1.head: صَنعاء
1.2.1.meaning: Sana'a, the Yemeni city where the travellers are addressed.

1.2.2.meaning: Turn aside, make a detour to someone.

2.1.2.head: زَهِدَ
2.1.2.meaning: Valued something too little to seek it.

2.2.4.head: مُبتَلىً
2.2.4.meaning: Put to the test, here by a companion’s need.

3.1.5.head: المَرخ
3.1.5.meaning: Al-Markh, a place name that is also the name of a tree.

3.2.4.head: ذَراني
3.2.4.meaning: Leave me be, addressed to both companions.

4.1.5.meaning: One taking aim, here fixing his gaze on her country.

4.2.2.head: إِنسان العَين
4.2.2.meaning: “The person of the eye”, the pupil in which a tiny reflected figure appears.

5.2.2.head: حاضِر
5.2.2.meaning: People camped at a water source, hence an encampment.

5.2.3.head: الرَّوحاء
5.2.3.meaning: Al-Rawha, a Hijazi stopping place on the Medina road.

6.1.2-3.head: جَسرَة الأَصلاب
6.1.2-3.meaning: “Strong of back”, a tall, sturdy she-camel.

6.1.4-5.head: ناجِيَة السُّرى
6.1.4-5.meaning: “Swift at night travel”, able to cover ground after dark.

6.2.4.head: وَخَدان
6.2.4.meaning: A quick camel gait with long strides.

7.1.1.meaning: Alight or call in briefly, said to two people.

7.1.3.head: عَفراء
7.1.3.meaning: Afra, Urwa’s cousin and beloved in the Udhri accounts.

7.2.1-2.head: شَحط النَّوى
7.2.1-2.meaning: “The remoteness of the destination”, distance imposed by parting.

8.1.2.head: واشٍ
8.1.2.meaning: A talebearer who betrays an intimacy, here addressed in the dual.

8.2.1-3.head: قَرَّت عَينُهُ
8.2.1-3.meaning: “His eye grew cool”, it found rest and delight in what it saw.

8.2.5.meaning: Leave me to myself, from the verb for entrusting something to another.

9.2.2-3.head: بُرد يَمنَة
9.2.2-3.meaning: A Yemeni mantle, here a pair of fine outer garments.

10.1.5.head: تَبَيَّنَ
10.1.5.meaning: Discerned clearly what had been hidden from sight.

10.2.2.head: ضُرّ
10.2.2.meaning: Affliction, here the wasting visible on his body.

11.1.4.head: عَظم
11.1.4.meaning: Bones, here thin enough to show the extent of his wasting.

11.2.4.head: خَفَقان
11.2.4.meaning: Fluttering, used of a racing heart and a beating wing.

12.1.6.head: قُرحَة
12.1.6.meaning: A sore or ulcer, imagined on the liver.

12.2.5.head: وَكَفَ
12.2.5.meaning: Dripped steadily, of rain or tears.

13.1.2.meaning: The one in whom he places most hope.

13.2.3-4.head: المُعرِض المُتَواني
13.2.3-4.meaning: “The one who turns away and delays”, grammatically masculine in one ancient explanation because ‘person’ is understood.

14.1.6.head: هَوى
14.1.6.meaning: A longing that draws one creature to another.

15.2.4.head: رُئِيَ
15.2.4.meaning: Were seen, in the passive: no watcher should catch sight of them.

16.1.2.head: ناقَة
16.1.2.meaning: The she-camel he rides, given a longing of her own.

16.1.4.head: قُدّام
16.1.4.meaning: Ahead of the traveller, the opposite direction from the camel’s longing.

17.1.5.head: مُعَرَّج
17.1.5.meaning: A place to turn aside to or stop at.

17.2.4.head: غُدُوّ
17.2.4.meaning: Setting out early in the day.

18.2.5.head: يَمانٍ
18.2.5.meaning: Yemeni, describing the lightning on the southern horizon.

19.1.5.head: ظَلَعَ
19.1.5.meaning: Limped under strain or from lameness.

19.2.5.head: يَدان
19.2.5.meaning: “Two hands”, in an idiom for having the strength to cope.

20.2.5.head: وَجَفَ
20.2.5.meaning: Quivered or throbbed from fear, here of their two livers.

21.1.5.head: شَحَطَ
21.1.5.meaning: Grew distant, said of a home whose people move away.

21.2.2-4.head: شُقَّتِ العَصا
21.2.2-4.meaning: “The staff was split”, a group or union broke apart.

22.1.5.head: عَذَلَ
22.1.5.meaning: Reproached a lover and pressed him to give up his attachment.

22.2.2.head: عِراقِيّ
22.2.2.meaning: Iraqi, here a longing directed towards Iraq.

25.1.2.head: قَطاة
25.1.2.meaning: A sandgrouse, a desert bird that travels far to water.

25.1.3.head: عُلِّقَ
25.1.3.meaning: Was suspended by one wing, leaving the other to struggle.

26.1.2-3.head: عَرّاف اليَمامَة
26.1.2-3.meaning: The healer of al-Yamama, tentatively identified in biographical accounts as Riyah ibn Kuhayla.

26.1.4.head: حُكم
26.1.4.meaning: The fee fixed at the healer’s own discretion.

26.2.2.head: نَجد
26.2.2.meaning: Najd, the central Arabian uplands, home to the second healer.

27.2.4.head: اِبتَدَرَ
27.2.4.meaning: Hastened to act, each eager to be first.

28.1.4.head: رُقيَة
28.1.4.meaning: A spoken healing charm or invocation.

28.2.2.head: سَلوَة
28.2.2.meaning: A draught supposed to bring forgetfulness of love.

29.2.2.head: ذَخَرَ
29.2.2.meaning: Kept something back instead of spending it.

29.2.5.head: أَلا
29.2.5.meaning: Fell short in effort, here explicitly denied of both healers.

30.2.2.head: ضُمِّنَ
30.2.2.meaning: Was made to contain something, here said of the ribs.

31.1.5.head: عِمَّة
31.1.5.meaning: A turban or the wrapping wound around the head.

31.2.4.head: اِلتاثَ
31.2.4.meaning: Wound the turban round the head.

32.2.2.head: دَفّ
32.2.2.meaning: The flank of a camel, here one on either side.

32.2.3.head: نِضوَة
32.2.3.meaning: A she-camel worn thin by travel.

32.2.4.head: عِدل
32.2.4.meaning: One of two matching packs hung on opposite flanks.

33.1.6-8.meaning: “May you never cease to be afflicted”, an imprecation.

33.2.1.head: حَليف
33.2.1.meaning: A sworn ally, here a lifelong companion of distress.

34.1.5.head: سَجِيَّة
34.1.5.meaning: A trait so settled that a person acts from it habitually.

35.1.4.head: حَسرَة
35.1.4.meaning: Grief at losing something one had hoped for.

36.2.2.head: مَقسوم
36.2.2.meaning: Divided up, as if the heart were scattered in pieces.

37.1.3.head: حَشر
37.1.3.meaning: The Gathering of all creatures after resurrection.

38.1.4-5.head: دِمنَة الدّار
38.1.4-5.meaning: “The camp’s trace”, marks left by a departed household.

38.2.4.head: اِنتَحَبَ
38.2.4.meaning: Sobbed aloud, here of a crow’s call.

39.2.3.head: وَكر
39.2.3.meaning: The nest or roost of a bird.

40.2.2.head: هَضَمَ
40.2.2.meaning: Took away piecemeal, here of eating into his sides.

41.2.2.head: طَعِمَ
41.2.2.meaning: Tasted or ate, said here of the other birds. Al-Qali’s text has “eat” in the same position.

41.2.5.head: وَذَرَ
41.2.5.meaning: Left behind, here the remains of the crows’ meal.

42.1.3.head: ذِكر
42.1.3.meaning: Remembrance of a person, set beside his public mentions of her.

43.1.4.head: واشٍ
43.1.4.meaning: An informer who carries a story to cause trouble.

43.2.3.head: خُلَّة
43.2.3.meaning: An intimate beloved, here used as a telltale’s allegation.

44.2.1.head: تَواشى
44.2.1.meaning: Passed malicious tales from one person to the next.

44.2.5.head: مَكان
44.2.5.meaning: His place or seat. In the Mu'nisa the corresponding word ends makaniya.

46.1.4.head: اليَمامَة
46.1.4.meaning: Al-Yamama, a district of central Arabia, here a remote home for a spy.

46.2.3.head: شُؤم
46.2.3.meaning: Ill omen, the evil consequences of the informer’s arrival.

47.1.4.head: بَكرَة
47.1.4.meaning: A young she-camel, the unit in which the bridewealth is reckoned. Al-Qali’s continuous text has the more general “she-camel”. Al-Baghdadi records both expressions.

47.2.6.head: ثَمانٍ
47.2.6.meaning: Eight she-camels, with the animals understood from the first half.

48.1.3.head: مَحيا
48.1.3.meaning: A life or lifetime, shared here by the pair.

48.2.5.head: كَفَن
48.2.5.meaning: A burial shroud, one for each of the two bodies.

49.2.1.head: خَلِيّ
49.2.1.meaning: Free from care or from another’s scrutiny.

50.1.4.head: مَنهَل
50.1.4.meaning: A watering place on a travelling route.

50.2.3-4.head: عُرَّة جَرَب
50.2.3-4.meaning: A skin disease of camels, here mange or a scabby condition.

51.2.4.head: فاهَ
51.2.4.meaning: Uttered something aloud, literally gave it mouth.

52.2.2.head: قَلوص
52.2.2.meaning: A young riding camel, here one for each traveller.

52.2.4.head: وَخَدَ
52.2.4.meaning: Travelled at a quick, extended stride.

53.1.1.head: ضُحَيّ
53.1.1.meaning: A diminutive of forenoon, narrowing down the hour he recalls.

53.1.3.head: جَنوب
53.1.3.meaning: A wind blowing from the south.

53.2.2.head: رَيّا
53.2.2.meaning: A fragrance carried on the breeze.

54.1.2.head: زَفرَة
54.1.2.meaning: Long breaths of distress. Ibn al-Anbari cites both occurrences here for their compressed pronunciation, zafrat.

54.2.4.head: عَشِيّ
54.2.4.meaning: Late day as evening draws near.

55.2.1.head: بِلال
55.2.1.meaning: A little moisture or a sip to wet the mouth.

55.2.3-5.head: زَلَّت بِهِ القَدَمان
55.2.3-5.meaning: “His two feet slipped”, he failed to stand by what was required of him.

56.1.1.head: مَنّى
56.1.1.meaning: Raised someone’s hopes by holding out a promise.

57.1.1.head: بُنَيَّة
57.1.1.meaning: A diminutive of ‘daughter’, affectionate in the phrase ‘my little cousin’.

57.2.4.head: صُرَد
57.2.4.meaning: A shrike, a predatory bird whose call he takes as an omen.

58.2.2.head: حَلِيَ
58.2.2.meaning: Found something delightful, whether to the eye or the tongue.

59.1.3-5.head: رآهُ في العَدُوّ
59.1.3-5.meaning: “Saw her among the enemy”, encountered the beloved inside hostile company.

60.1.2.head: هابَ
60.1.2.meaning: Stood in awe of someone, combining fear and respect.

60.2.5-6.head: شَباة السِّنان
60.2.5-6.meaning: “The edge of the spearpoint”, its sharp penetrating tip.

61.2.2.head: رِواق
61.2.2.meaning: A curtain or hanging extended along a side of a tent.

61.2.4.head: خَلَق
61.2.4.meaning: Threadbare from use, here of both hangings.

62.1.1.head: خُلَيق
62.1.1.meaning: A little rag. The diminutive makes the two threadbare hangings of his uncle’s tent sound more contemptible.

62.1.2.head: هَلهال
62.1.2.meaning: Loosely woven, with gaps between the threads.

62.2.4.head: يَرَقان
62.2.4.meaning: Grubs or caterpillars. The classical apparatus also notes an irregular case vowel at the rhyme.

63.1.2.head: هَفّاف
63.1.2.meaning: Light enough to flutter in a slight wind.

63.2.3.head: ريح
63.2.3.meaning: Winds, an old plural of rih in this context.

63.2.4.head: اِصطَفَقَ
63.2.4.meaning: Struck together with a clapping sound.

64.1.3.head: أَظعان
64.1.3.meaning: Women travelling in camel litters, or the litters themselves.

64.1.5-6.head: رَونَق الضُّحى
64.1.5-6.meaning: “The sheen of forenoon”, the clear brightness of the morning.

64.2.3-4.head: نَهّاضَة الخَدَيان
64.2.3-4.meaning: A she-camel quick to rise and stride briskly forward.

65.1.6.head: غِرَّة
65.1.6.meaning: An unguarded moment in which nobody is watching.

65.2.4.head: يَسَر
65.2.4.meaning: Easy or yielding, here of their two dispositions. Al-Zamakhshari glosses the word as “both easy, readily yielding” in a parallel verse by Ibn Muqbil.

66.1.4-5.head: خَفّاقَة الحَشا
66.1.4-5.meaning: “Fluttering of flank”, an old expression for a slender waist.

66.2.3.head: قاذورَة
66.2.3.meaning: Fastidious aversion, the forbidding manner of her father.

66.2.4.head: شَنَآن
66.2.4.meaning: Violent dislike or hostility, colouring the description of her father.

67.1.2.head: وِشاح
67.1.2.meaning: An ornamental sash, often beaded, worn across a woman’s body.

67.2.2-3.head: عِنانا مُهرَة
67.2.2-3.meaning: “A filly’s two reins”, the two straps by which she is guided.

68.1.2.head: بَدَن
68.1.2.meaning: A body garment or short tunic against which the two sashes meet.

68.2.1.head: مَثنىً
68.2.1.meaning: The bend or doubled part of something long and flexible.

69.1.2.head: حِقف
69.1.2.meaning: A curved sandhill, here one of the two curves of the hips.

69.2.1.head: قِطار
69.2.1.meaning: Raindrops. Rain accounts for the packed sand here. Al-Qawwal takes the same word as a string of camels.

69.2.3.head: الجَوزاء
69.2.3.meaning: Al-Jawza, the stars of Orion, whose setting was associated with rain. Al-Qawwal gives another sense of the word, a black ewe with a white middle.

69.2.4.head: اِلتَبَدَ
69.2.4.meaning: Became matted or compact, here of sand firmed by rain.

70.2.2.head: أَلَجَّ
70.2.2.meaning: Made something persist, here kept the eye shedding tears.

71.1.1.head: عَين
71.1.1.meaning: His own two eyes. Al-Qali’s text has “and two eyes”, without the possessive ending.

71.1.3-4.head: أَوفى نَشزاً
71.1.3-4.meaning: “Mounted a rise”, gained higher ground for a view.

71.2.1.head: مَأق
71.2.1.meaning: The inner corner of the eye, where tears gather.

72.2.4.head: اِبتَدَرَ
72.2.4.meaning: Raced to get ahead, here of the eyes outdoing each other.

73.1.2.head: حادٍ
73.1.2.meaning: A camel-driver who urges the animals on with his voice.

73.2.4.head: اِرعَوى
73.2.4.meaning: Desisted or drew back, here checked the pace at his call.

74.1.2-3.head: التّالي القَطوف
74.1.2-3.meaning: “The slow follower”, the animal lagging at the rear.

74.1.5.meaning: Flagged or grew slack on the road.

74.2.1.head: مُشيح
74.2.1.meaning: Hurrying on in earnest, also alert or wary.

75.1.5.head: رُميَ
75.1.5.meaning: Was struck, a past form expressing a wish that illness strike them.

76.2.1.head: سِربال
76.2.1.meaning: A shirt or tunic enclosing the body.

76.2.4.head: قَطِران
76.2.4.meaning: Tar or pitch, a sticky substance also used to dress camels’ skin.

77.1.4.head: وَيل
77.1.4.meaning: Ruin or bitter grief. Here it describes the woe he has just named. Al-Qali has an accusative which repeats the cry of woe.

78.2.1-2.head: نَعام وَبِرك
78.2.1-2.meaning: Na'am and Birk, two places in this reading. Al-Qali also gives the words ‘yes’ and ‘no’.

79.1.5.head: وَجد
79.1.5.meaning: The intensity of love and grief at separation.

79.2.2.head: جِنّ
79.2.2.meaning: Jinn, unseen beings imagined here to have a lover to match the human one.

80.1.3.head: ثُمَّتَ
80.1.3.meaning: An extended form of ‘then’, marking the lover’s turn to speak.

80.2.1.head: أَضعَفَ
80.2.1.meaning: Multiplied. The past verb answers the “if” in the preceding verse, as his own love exceeds the measure of the other two combined.

81.1.4.head: وَعى
81.1.4.meaning: Grasped or retained the sense of what someone said.

81.2.3.head: ناجى
81.2.3.meaning: Spoke privately or confided in someone.

82.2.2.head: غُراب
82.2.2.meaning: A crow, recalling the pair at the camp. Ibn al-Jawzi transmits ‘eagle’ here.

82.2.4.head: خَفَقان
82.2.4.meaning: Repeated wingbeats, echoing the palpitation of the heart.
